         SAVE THE LAMPASAS’ BRIEF IN RESPONSE TO SOAH ORDER NO. 35

         Save the Lampasas submits this Brief in Response to State Office of Administrative

  Hearings (SOAH) Order No. 35, which requested that the parties submit responses by October 7,

  2026.1 Accordingly, this Brief is timely filed.

                                           I.   RESPONSE

         SOAH Order No. 35 directs the parties to submit briefing on two issues from the Public

  Utility Commission of Texas’ (Commission or PUC) Preliminary Order as referenced in the

  Commission’s Order on Remand:

        Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal reliability
         standards? [Preliminary Order Issue No. 11]; and

        What is the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from the
         proposed transmission facilities considering both current and future expected congestion
         levels and the ability of the proposed transmission facilities to reduce those congestion
         levels? [Preliminary Order Issue No. 13].




         1
             SOAH Order No. 35 Requiring Briefing on Remanded Issue Nos. 11 and 13 and Denying Kevin
  Kennedy’s September 20 Motion (Sept. 22, 2026).
                                                                                           Page 2 of 9


       These two issues appear in the Commission’s Preliminary Order under the heading of

“Cost to Consumers.”2 Traditionally, these issues are addressed to ensure that the cost of the

proposed project is warranted when balanced against the basis of need for the proposed project

as asserted by the applicant(s). The original Proposal for Decision (PFD) addressed both issues

in a manner consistent with the Preliminary Order and briefing in this proceeding under the

heading Cost to Consumers. 3

       Additional legal context is provided here. PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission to

consider a specific set of factors bearing on need, and 16 Texas Administration Code

§ 25.101(b)(3) further divides the need determination into three distinct pathways, economic,

reliability, and resiliency, each with its own evidentiary requirements. The applicant bears the

burden of producing evidence on these statutory and regulatory factors. Towards this end, the

Commission’s Standard Application for a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for a

Proposed Transmission Line provides that an applicant may demonstrate need by describing:

       . . . the existing transmission system and conditions addressed by this application.
       For projects that are planned to accommodate load growth, provide historical load
       data and load projections for at least five years. For projects to accommodate load
       growth or to address reliability issues, provide a description of the steady-state
       load flow analysis that justifies the project. For interconnection projects, provide
       any documentation from a transmission service customer, generator, transmission
       service provider, or other entity to establish that the proposed facilities are
       needed.4

Practically, need is demonstrated through five kinds of projects, those needed for (1) the bulk

power system (the reliability standard), (2) generation interconnection, (3) load growth, (4) cost

reduction under the production cost savings test, or (5) cost reduction due to economic

congestion relief.


       2
           Order of Referral and Preliminary Order at 10 (Mar. 30, 2026).
       3
           SOAH Proposal for Decision with Memorandum at 148-150 (Aug. 20, 2026) (PFD).
       4
           See, e.g. Applicants’ Ex. 1 (Application) at 19.
                                                                                            Page 3 of 9


        The Applicants bear the burden of proving that evidence supports their claimed basis of

need. In this case, the Applicants claimed that the Permian Basin Reliability Plan’s (PBPR)

serves as the evidence supporting need for a bundle of proposed transmission line projects

including local upgrades and the creation of new significant regional upgrades identified as

“import paths” to facilitate bulk power transfer to the Permian Basin region. 5 As the present

application is for an “import path project,” the basis for need is identified as serving the bulk

power system as a reliability project.6 This conclusion is supported by the Applicants’ statement

that “Import Path 2 is a reliability project.” 7

        A.         Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal
                   reliability standards? [Preliminary Order Issue No. 11]

        The PFD properly analyzed and answered Preliminary Order Issue No. 11, based on the

record evidence in the Application filed in this proceeding. 8 In fact, the Applicants’ Initial Brief

specifically addressed Preliminary Order Issue No. 11 as follows: 9




        5
            Application at 22.
        6
            Id.
        7
            Applicants’ Reply Brief at 24 (Jun. 26, 2026).
        8
            PFD at 149.
        9
            Applicants’ Initial Brief at 51.
                                                                                          Page 4 of 9


        There is no dispute that the Applicants present this application as a reliability project –

therefore not requiring a separate cost-benefit analysis.     What is disputed, however, is the

determination in the PFD that the Applicants have failed to meet their burden of proof to present

evidence sufficient to demonstrate the proposed project is necessary to satisfy state and federal

reliability standards.

        The Proposal for Decision provides a thorough analysis of the evidence in the record

relevant to the claimed need for this project as a reliability project. The PFD provides this

helpful summary of the key evidentiary points that support the recommendation that the

Applicants have failed to meet their burden of proof with regard to the Application’s claimed

need for this project to address reliability of the grid:

        First, Applicants did not present a case for the need for Import Path 2 separate and
        apart from the three 765-kV import paths as one comprehensive project. But the
        PBRP initiative is unlike the CREZ initiative where the Legislature determined
        need for one comprehensive project, the CREZ transmission lines. No such
        Legislative need determination was made for the PBRP transmission lines.
        Instead, under HB 5066, Applicants had to show Import Path 2 is independently
        necessary under the PURA § 37.056 factors. They did not.

        Second, Applicants failed to show the PBRP’s underlying projected loads
        establish a need for Import Path 2. Instead, the record proves that the projected
        loads—because of changed circumstances—do not support these proposed
        transmission Projects but instead should be re-evaluated.

        Third, Applicants failed to prove that sufficient power is available at Bell County
        East to transmit westward via Import Path 2 and, thus, failed to prove Import 2’s
        stated function of moving power to the Permin Basin. Instead, the record
        establishes that neither Applicants nor ERCOT determined whether the central
        Texas region’s net generation is sufficient to serve Import Path 2.

        Fourth, intervenors submitted credible evidence of an alternative analysis—new
        and planned gas generation in the Permian Basin—that could reduce or eliminate
        the need for Import Path 2, thereby justifying the Commission’s consideration of
        this alternative.10




        10
             PFD at 99.
                                                                                                       Page 5 of 9


        As thoroughly addressed in the PFD, the evidence shows changed circumstances that call

into question the assumptions underlying the Permian Basin Reliability Plan and, in turn, the

reliance on this ERCOT Report as the cornerstone for showing the “reliability need” for Import

Path 2.11 Further, as discussed in the PFD, the record evidence shows: “[t]here are real questions

as to whether this particular project will allow new power to be brought to that load.” 12

However, the Applicants have failed to introduce sufficient evidence to carry the burden of proof

on this claim.

        The ERCOT Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBPR) Study proposed the Bell East to Big

Hill transmission line to address a projected need to meet the reliability criteria in 2038. 13

However, the report also recommends that the Commission wait until more information is

provided in the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan (RTP) before committing to the 765kV

transmission projects.14

        The 2024 Regional Transmission Plan did not show how this project would meet a

defined reliability standard for 2030.15 Instead, the 2024 RTP states the project was developed

“to facilitate the PUC’s discussion . . . to address statewide reliability needs.” 16 Towards that

end, the 2024 RTP states that “[t]he start case for the 765-kV plan incorporated all local projects

needed by 2030 in the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, along with the three Permian Basin 765-

                                                                                                          Page 6 of 9


kV import paths.”17 ERCOT’s 2024 RTP included the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) in

its planning assumptions, but it did not provide any reasoned justification or analysis that Import

Path 2 meets any reliability standard.

        The ERCOT 2024 RTP and PBRP provide thorough and invaluable information that

helped the Commission choose between 345-kV and 765-kV Permian Basin transmission

options. Neither document nor testimony provides sufficient evidence that Import Path 2 is

needed before 2038, which is outside the short- and long-term planning timeline for both

ERCOT and NERC. The Applicants rely heavily on the PBPR to support their assertions of

need.   The analysis underlying the cited ERCOT PBPR was performed in 2024, and the

conclusory testimony to which it is attached does not support Oncor’s assertion that the present

project meets state or federal reliability standards.18 The Commission’s obligation to determine

whether the line is needed for the convenience and necessity of the public differs from the

standard of review of need undertaken at ERCOT.19 As determined by the Commission, the

utilities had the obligation to address need for each project in the individual CCN cases. This is

consistent with the statutory obligations for the Commission to consider ERCOT's

recommendation, but to not bound by the ERCOT Report, and to consider all relevant factors

introduced into evidence in the case, including and changed circumstances. 20

        The answer to Issue No. 11 is that while the Applicants' claimed basis of need for this

project asserts potential reliability concerns in the 2030 and 2038 analyses performed in the

PBPR, the Applicants have failed to meet their burden of proof with regard to this claimed basis

Comparison) at 3 (Jan. 24, 2025).

of need and have failed to produce an analysis sufficient to demonstrate that the specific project

proposed in this case is needed to resolve any state or federal reliability criteria.

        Accordingly, the Supplemental PFD could include the following finding:

        The Application presents this project as one that is proposed to meet
        address future reliability needs; however, the Applicants failed to meet
        their burden of proof to establish that the proposed project is needed to
        address federal or state reliability standards.

With this finding, consistent with Commission precedent, the Commission should deny the

application without prejudice to refiling after updated analysis by ERCOT and the Applicants to

incorporate the changes that affect the forecasted load numbers that were used in the PBRP.

This revised analysis could and should also incorporate consideration of the end point of the

proposed project after consideration of the applicable statutory factors and physical features of

the affected landscape and communities.21

        B.         What is the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result
                   from the proposed transmission facilities considering both current and
                   future expected congestion levels and the ability of the proposed transmission
                   facilities to reduce those congestion levels? [Preliminary Order Issue No. 13]

        The PFD properly analyzed and answered Preliminary Order Issue No. 13, stating that

the “Applicants did not submit the information called for by the cost issues-neither the estimated

cost of the facilities to consumers nor the estimated congestion cost savings to consumers.” 22

This conclusion is supported by the Applicants’ Initial Brief on Preliminary Order Issue No. 13,

which is shown here in its entirety:23

        In their reply brief, the Applicants point out that congestion cost savings are not required

to be introduced in the application for a reliability project: 24




        Accordingly, the Supplemental PFD could include the following additional finding:

                 The Application addressed this project as a reliability project and
                 asserted no justification for the project based on current or future
                 congestion levels or the ability of the proposed project to reduce
                 those congestion levels.

Review of Chapter § 25.101 Certification Criteria, Project No. 53403, Order Adopting Amendments to 16 TAC
§ 25.101 as Approved at the November 30, 2022 Open Meeting at 17 (Dec. 7, 2022) (reliability projects “are not
required to pass the congestion cost savings test.”).
                                                                                      Page 9 of 9


                                       II.   CONCLUSION

       Save the Lampasas respectfully submits this Brief in Response to SOAH Order No. 35

and supports the addition of supplemental findings to the PFD as suggested here without change

to the original recommendation that the pending application be denied without prejudice to

potential refiling after updated analysis.

               e. Import Path 2 is a Reliability Project, Not an Economic Project

               Leif Allred and Laura Pressley argue that the Application is deficient, because it does not

       contain the phrase "congestion cost savings."124 That omission is intentional and immaterial. A

       transmission project may be classified as either a reliability project or an economic project, and

       Import Path 2 is a reliability project to address the needs identified in the Permian Basin Reliability

       Plan.   Under the Commission's own rule, reliability projects are expressly exempt from the

       economic tests, including the congestion cost savings test. 125




        Accordingly, the Supplemental PFD could include the following additional finding:

                 The Application addressed this project as a reliability project and
                 asserted no justification for the project based on current or future
                 congestion levels or the ability of the proposed project to reduce
                 those congestion levels.
